name: Erik Weber

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, AI firms, unions, government or political parties, and we don't sell anything or campaign. This conversation is confidential, so you can separate what you'd say publicly from your private thoughts. Could you describe a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm Erik, 43, and I handle ordinary wiring and electrical repairs in homes and businesses. I've got a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, years of experience and about average skill, not a management or specialist role. My pay is above the usual rate; my partner drives a forklift, and we have children aged eleven and sixteen, a mortgage and nine months of expenses saved. There are plenty of other electrical firms nearby, and I use AI daily for checked notes and parts descriptions, without letting it decide electrical safety.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a tool can be useful without winning an argument about the whole future. I use AI every day to organise my checked work notes and compare parts descriptions. I'd still rather find the actual fault than win the lunchroom prediction contest.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage and my partner's regular wage cover the household comfortably, and we've got nine months of expenses saved. My pay is above the usual rate, and there are plenty of other electrical firms nearby. Nothing in that mild picture makes me think our mortgage or ordinary living is in danger.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the house and business repair calls. Starting now I'd continue comparing AI-sorted notes with my test readings and the actual part before anything went into a customer handover. Through the first year I'd keep the same work and family budget rather than make an experiment simply because I was bored.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and still curious. I'd be happy with a tool that saves me a little time and leaves the evening free. Not every improvement needs its own speech.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What experience are you bringing to those repairs?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm 43, with a vocational certificate and an electrician's licence, and I've done the ordinary jobs for years. I'm about average at the trade, not a specialist in every control system. When the problem goes outside my experience, I get the right person rather than ask the computer to make me confident.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who shares the family budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My partner drives a forklift in a warehouse, and our children are eleven and sixteen. We've got a mortgage, and the reserve came from years of putting something aside. I like trying tools early, but that doesn't make the household account my experimental budget.

say: I'd value **useful tools** without turning every improvement into a prediction contest.
I'd focus on the **actual fault** and a correct customer handover rather than an impressive-looking draft.
think: Our **regular wages** cover the mortgage and living costs, with nine months of expenses saved.
My **higher pay** and plenty of nearby electrical firms make this mild picture feel secure.
do: Keep completing **house and business repairs** through the first year.
Continue checking daily **AI-sorted notes** against test readings and actual parts before customer handovers.
feel: **Calm** about household finances, with curiosity that stays separate from a need for dramatic change.
S0.quote: I like trying tools early, but that doesn't make the household account my experimental budget.
fieldNote: His **current security** follows covered bills, two regular wages, higher pay and a nine-month reserve rather than a claim of exceptional skill.
His **daily AI use** remains checked against physical evidence, with an explicit boundary around unfamiliar specialist work and family money.

steps.text: Keep ordinary repairs and daily handovers checked against readings and actual parts

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say let's measure a small change properly before calling it a new way of working. I'd volunteer to try the approved stock-list tool on the three common fittings we keep running out of. I'd share the bad counts as well as the minutes saved.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own wage looks safe over the next few years because our repair work is physical and the diary is full. My partner's forklift work is also physical, though I won't promise either job survives forever. With the reserve behind us, this sounds more like a useful change to try than a threat to our living.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the owner this week for a four-week paid AI stock-list trial with my normal wage and hours unchanged. I'd learn the new tool by comparing its counts with the shelf and checking every draft reorder before the office approved it. In the first year I'd keep doing repairs and stop the stock tool if mistakes or checking time outweighed the benefit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, and quite keen to start. A test that lets me stop after a bad result is a pleasure, not a promise I've trapped myself inside. I'd still want to get home when I said I would.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why start with only three fittings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because I can count them, see the empty space and check whether the suggestion matches real use. I'd rather learn from something small than hide a bad result inside a thousand lines. The office would still approve an order, not a machine spending the firm's money alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the trial had to happen in your unpaid evenings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then I'd ask for paid time or not do it. I can be interested without donating my children's evening to the firm's stock cupboard. The normal wage and hours would be agreed before I started.

say: I'd measure a **small stock trial** before calling it a new way of working.
I'd show **wrong counts** as honestly as any time saved by the tool.
think: My **repair wage** looks secure over the next few years with physical work and a full diary.
My partner's **forklift work** is also hands-on, with the reserve supporting confidence rather than permanent safety.
do: Request a **four-week paid trial** now with normal wage and hours unchanged.
Learn the **stock-list tool** on three fittings, comparing shelf counts and checking drafts before office order approval.
Keep **repairs** during the first year and stop the tool if mistakes or checking time outweigh benefits.
feel: **Calm** about own livelihood and interested in a bounded trial with an honest stopping point.
S1.quote: I can be interested without donating my children's evening to the firm's stock cupboard.
fieldNote: He expects **near-term wage security** in both physical jobs, making the trial useful rather than a response to expected household income loss.
The **new tool learning** has paid-time and unchanged-wage conditions, physical count checks and human order approval rather than unchecked purchasing.

steps.text: Learn stock tool in four paid weeks with normal wage hours retained and office-approved orders
Keep physical repairs and stop stock trial if errors or checking time outweigh benefit

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say thinking AI arrives in 2028 and capable robots around 2031, so we should use the interval without pretending hands-on work is permanent shelter. I'd tell the family I wanted to test a small business while I still had wages. I'd explain the limits before showing anybody a clever booking page.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My paid hours could shrink once robots compete for ordinary installations, and my partner's forklift work could face the same physical change. Nine months saved gives us room, not two replacement careers. I don't know the machines' prices or how fast employers buy them, so I want a small test rather than bet on a date when our wages stop.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd check my employment terms, permissions, insurance and full setup costs now for a small weekend electrical-repair service within my licence. I'd offer two Saturday slots monthly only with my partner's agreement and all setup costs within 900 of spare earnings, leaving our nine-month reserve untouched. In the first year after 2028 I'd keep my paid job and stop the sideline after three bookings whose receipts failed to cover their costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the household's later earnings, but interested in a test I can stop. A few paying customers wouldn't make me immune to robots. I'd want evidence of demand before I called myself ready for anything.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the 900 include insurance and permissions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Every setup cost, not just the tools I enjoy buying. If the quoted costs didn't fit, I wouldn't open the repair service. I won't borrow money to make a weekend repair business look affordable. My partner's agreement and the untouched reserve are conditions, not promises I'd revisit after spending.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the employer did not permit outside repair work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Then the service wouldn't start while those terms applied. I'd keep the current wage rather than hide weekend jobs from the firm. The test is meant to add a choice, not turn a secure job into a dispute.

say: I'd explain **2028 thinking AI** and robots around 2031 without promising permanent protection for physical work.
I'd discuss **business limits** with the family before showing off a booking page.
think: Both household **physical wages** could shrink once robots compete for electrical and forklift tasks.
Our **nine-month reserve** gives room to test, while machine prices and employer purchase timing remain unknown.
do: Check **employment terms**, permissions, insurance and full setup costs before any outside electrical work within my licence.
Offer **two monthly Saturdays** only with partner consent, all setup within 900 spare earnings and the nine-month reserve untouched.
Keep the **paid job** after 2028 and stop the sideline after three bookings whose receipts fail to cover costs.
feel: **Anxious** about later household income, with control through a bounded test and no claim of robot immunity.
S2.quote: I won't borrow money to make a weekend repair business look affordable.
fieldNote: His **side-income test** stays within an ordinary electrician's licence, with employment terms, permissions and insurance checked before opening.
The **all-in cap** comes from spare earnings, requires partner consent and leaves the nine-month reserve untouched; three losing bookings trigger stopping.

steps.text: Offer two Saturday slots monthly, permitted, insured, within licence, partner consent, 900 spare-earnings cap, reserve untouched
Keep paid job after 2028 and stop sideline after three bookings failing costs

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years lets a small idea earn the right to grow instead of making it the family's rescue on day one. Thinking AI arrives in 2031 and robots around 2034, so the physical service still has the same longer risk. I'd keep ordinary wages while testing whether customers actually pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My own earnings look secure over the next few years while the repair diary stays full, and the reserve gives us room to judge demand. I wouldn't treat a second electrical service as independent of the same robot competition. More time makes it easier to stop a poor idea before relying on it, not easier to call every idea safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start only the same permitted two-Saturday service, with my partner's consent, the all-in 900 spare-earnings cap and the reserve untouched. After three profitable bookings I'd trial an AI draft-booking page using made-up appointments first, personally confirming every real visit and quote. In the first year after 2031 I'd keep my paid job, committing no household setup money beyond the cap and stopping the service after three bookings that failed to cover costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy about the longer market, with patience to check a test. I like building something, but I'd want the figures in a plain notebook my partner could read too. A good-looking page doesn't make an appointment paid work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the booking page needed a monthly subscription?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It would have to fit inside the same 900 setup limit, with later costs covered by real receipts rather than the household reserve. If that didn't work, I'd use the phone and paper diary. Automating a booking isn't worth turning a small test into a permanent bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave employment after three successful bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, three bookings tell me the service can have customers, not replace a family wage. I'd keep the paid job and the two-slot limit. I'd need a much longer and different plan before discussing any reduction in employment with my partner.

I'd explain that **robots around 2034** still reach physical electrical work despite a different business arrangement.
think: My **near-term earnings** look secure with a full repair diary and reserve behind us.
The **sideline** faces the same robot competition, so extra time is for testing rather than assuming permanent safety.
do: Start only the **permitted Saturday service**, with partner consent, all setup within 900 spare earnings and the reserve untouched.
Trial **AI draft bookings** only after three profitable jobs, with test appointments, personal confirmations and all costs within the cap.
Keep **employment and two slots** after 2031, funding later costs from receipts and stopping after three bookings fail to cover costs.
feel: **Uneasy** about later competition, with patience to test demand and no rush to replace a family wage.
S3.quote: A good-looking page doesn't make an appointment paid work.
fieldNote: His **booking automation** is a new bounded activity after evidence of demand, retaining test data, personal visit confirmation and manual quoting decisions.
The **business limits** persist after success: two monthly slots, paid employment, partner consent, an untouched reserve and the same cost-based stop rule.

Trial AI bookings after three profitable jobs: test dummy appointments first, personally confirm visits/quotes within cap
Keep employment after 2031; stop after three bookings whose receipts fail to cover costs
Fund ongoing business costs only from paid receipts, never household reserves

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time to decide what a family wants from work as well as what the tools can do. I'd keep experimenting within a limit, but I'd protect the afternoons I promised the children. Thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 still arrive before I'd assume I can stop earning.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd be 53 in 2036 and about 56 when robots followed, so retirement isn't a checked answer. Our current wages, nine-month reserve and plenty of local firms make the next few years feel secure. I can enjoy that without promising that my job, the sideline or my partner's work lasts forever.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the paid job now and test the same two monthly repair slots only after checks, partner consent and all setup costs within 900 spare earnings, leaving the reserve untouched. I'd trial AI draft booking only after three profitable jobs, using made-up appointments first and personally confirming visits and quotes within the same cost limit. In the first year after 2036 I'd keep employment, pay ongoing business costs only from receipts and stop the service after three bookings failing to cover costs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm about the next few years, and still curious about the longer future. I'd like a tool to give time back rather than make me fill every Saturday with work. The family shouldn't have to prove we're preparing by never enjoying the present.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the service take more than two Saturdays if demand was strong?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not under the plan I've agreed with my partner. We'd have to discuss both the money and the family time again before changing the limit. A customer asking for an extra Saturday doesn't mean my family has agreed.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would tell you to stop an experiment before three losing bookings?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A safety or permission problem would stop it straight away, as would losing my partner's agreement or needing household reserve money. The three-booking rule is for checking costs, not permission to ignore those other limits. I'd keep the ordinary job and deal with the problem first.

S4.quote: A customer asking for an extra Saturday doesn't mean my family has agreed.

The **stop conditions** override revenue hopes: safety, permissions, partner consent and reserve protection apply before the cost-based three-booking rule.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because both household jobs involve physical work that capable robots around 2031 could reach. A clear account of actual paid hours and business costs would help, along with practical teaching on systems we really use. I'd want enough room to test an idea without telling the family it already replaces a wage.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask whose time gets used when somebody says a tool makes a small business easy. A neat booking page doesn't collect the children or finish a safe repair. I want my partner involved before my hobby becomes the family's extra shift.

headlineQuote: A neat booking page doesn't collect the children or finish a safe repair.
portrait: Erik is **43**, an experienced electrician with a vocational certificate and licence, average skill, higher pay and nine months of expenses saved.
His **partner drives a forklift**, with two school-age children, a mortgage and plenty of local electrical employers supporting present options.
He uses **AI daily**, but separates verified work and physical safety from attractive drafts or hopes about the future.
His **weekend-business test** requires permissions, partner consent, a 900 spare-earnings cap, an untouched reserve and a clear cost-based stop rule.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** leaves less preparation time before capable robots around 2031 could affect both adults' physical-work incomes.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **paid-hour and cost information** would help the family judge actual choices.
Practical teaching on **systems actually used** and room for limited tests would help without assuming replacement income.
